name: Plain dress

card.summary: A modest, unadorned dress code kept by Anabaptist, Quaker and other groups, giving a deliberately simple look free of trends and ornament.
card.note: A religious practice; this entry documents it as a style.

quick.overview:
Plain dress is clothing of modest design, sturdy fabric and conservative cut worn by groups such as the Amish, Mennonites, Hutterites, Brethren and Quakers. Garments are typically undecorated, in muted colours, and carry no logos.

As a look, it is minimal and uniform. Members describe it as signalling humility, identity and separation from fashion trends.
quick.how: Women often wear cape dresses with long skirts and head coverings; men wear dark trousers with suspenders and plain shirts, sometimes broad-brimmed hats. Many garments are handmade.
quick.risks: There are no physical risks. Plain clothing can be hard to find in mainstream shops.

lead: Plain dress is a practice among some religious groups, mainly Christian churches, of wearing modest clothing in sturdy fabric and conservative cut. It signals modesty, traditional gender roles, readiness for work, and communal identity, and keeps members apart from changing fashion [1].

Groups include Amish, Mennonites, Hutterites and Brethren, Conservative Quakers, and holiness Methodists, among others [1]. Garments are usually handmade, undecorated and free of trademarks, and the practice can extend to hair and beards [1]. As an appearance approach it is a minimal, uniform aesthetic.

chain: Muted solid colours and simple cuts
angle.text: The look is built on solid dark or neutral colours, straight cuts and no ornament, which gives a modest, tidy appearance.

paras: Women's garments include a long-sleeved, long-skirted cape dress and a kapp or veil based on 1 Corinthians 11; men's include trousers with suspenders, no neckties, and fabrics in black, white, grey and brown, with broad-brimmed hats among Quakers [1].

Early Quaker leader George Fox urged plain fashions; John Wesley's sermon 'On Dress' gave guidance to Methodists [1]. Theological reasons cite passages on modesty; sociological reasons include community identity and protection from attention, with Elizabeth Fry calling plain dress 'a hedge against the world' [1]. Variations are governed by community rules called ordnung [1].
